results.one_line: BiH bookkeepers, accountants and real estate agents are being inspected now on AML documents that no state portal or local product produces, and Croatia's A-count (EUR 281-540 a year) shows the product works and sells. A cheaper BiH version for about 3,000 obliged micro firms could make about 135,000-225,000 KM a year by year 3.
results.competitor_check: I found no BiH AML product for small obliged entities. Paragraf Lex seminars cost 175.50-198.90 KM with VAT and include no templates. SRR FBiH offers only booklets. Forvis Mazars sells consulting in Serbia with no public price. A-count (Croatia) does the whole job for Croatian law: free for up to 5 clients, EUR 281 a year for up to 20 clients, EUR 540 a year unlimited. That is reasonable for Croatia, but it has no BiH law or language variant. It is an entry threat and a price anchor, not an incumbent.
results.revenue:
The working base is 3,000 obliged small entities. Bookkeepers are about 2,500-2,700, scaled from Serbia's 5,476 registered accounting providers by population (unverified). Real estate agencies are about 250-350 (FBiH has 135). Auditors and dealers come on top.
- Base: 3,000 x 10% x 450 KM = 135,000 KM (about EUR 69k).
- Good: 3,000 x 15% x 500 KM = 225,000 KM (about EUR 115k).
- Low: 2,000 x 6% x 350 KM = 42,000 KM.
Expansion to other countries in the region is not counted.
results.ease: High to build and onboard. The product is a wizard, a document generator, a client register, sanctions-list checks and reminders, with no state integration. One developer plus an AML lawyer could ship it in 2-3 months. Selling is medium. The triggers are strong: FUZIP inspections run to end-2026, RS checks are ongoing, and the June 2026 FATF grey listing keeps pressure on. The channels are concentrated (SRR FBiH, the RS accountants' association, Paragraf seminars). Against that, buyers are price-sensitive and resent the duty. Three variants are needed: FBiH, RS and Brcko.

results.one_line: Mexican guard firms must keep a staff, uniform, vehicle and arms register and file monthly reports to the DGSP (first 10 days of the month) and to states (for example, Baja California's 8-part pack sent by email with Excel files). No software builds these reports, so a small Spanish register-plus-report tool at about MXN 3,000 a month has a real opening. The market is a soft count of a few thousand firms, and the federal filing channel is still unknown.
results.gap: There is no real portal. Baja California firms download formats and email a monthly pack every month, even when nothing changed. The pack holds an altas list, one cédula per leaver, a copy of the payroll or SUA, an Excel cardex, a fee receipt, an activity report and an Excel arms summary. The guide warns that the cardex, the state system and the payroll must match exactly, and that every field must be filled. Tamaulipas has a similar 5-business-day monthly report. In the 2026 DGSP sanctions, firms were punished for register gaps found during inspections: unreported altas and bajas (114 bajas at Multisistemas Uribe), training not reported within the first 10 days (Oblak), and uniforms and manager data (COSSEPPA, MXN 117,310). Software can fix this with one staff master that feeds payroll, the cardex and the cédulas, plus deadline tracking, exam and CUIP expiry alerts, an audit trail, an inspection pack, and multi-state, multi-client work for gestores.
results.competitor_check: No Mexican product for security-firm compliance was found in three Spanish searches. C-Guard Pro (USD 5 per user per month) does patrols, GPS, rounds, shifts and payroll, with no DGSP, CUIP, state report or REPSE features. GuardsPro (USD 5-10 per user per month) adds only licence-expiry alerts. Aspel NOI and CONTPAQi are payroll tools, so they are data sources rather than rivals. The real incumbent is the in-house or outside gestor, who works by hand and publishes no fees. The incumbents are partial, which makes this an opening and not a killer.
results.price: Per firm: MXN 1,500 a month base for up to 50 staff, plus MXN 10 per extra active staff, plus MXN 500 for each extra state report. A 150-guard firm in 2 states pays about MXN 3,000 a month (MXN 36,000 a year, about USD 2,000). That is about a third of one 2026 fine of MXN 113k-170k. Per gestor or consultant: about MXN 5,000 a month for up to 15 client firms (unverified).
results.revenue: The buyer counts are soft: AMESP says 8,000+ firms, and a trade article says about 3,300 registered firms, with 1,090 federal and 2,266 state authorisations in 2012 (unverified). I assume 2,000 firms with 30+ staff that can pay. Base case: 2,000 x 6% = 120 firms x MXN 36,000 = MXN 4.32M, plus 22 gestors x MXN 60,000 = MXN 1.32M, for about MXN 5.6M (about USD 310k). Low case: 50 firms x MXN 30,000 + 8 gestors x MXN 60,000 = about MXN 2.0M (USD 110k). High case: 3,500 x 6% = 210 firms x MXN 36,000 + MXN 1.32M = about MXN 8.9M (USD 490k).
results.ease: Medium. The build is easy: a small data model (people, equipment, branches, dated changes) and Excel and PDF output in fixed state formats, with no government API needed. Onboarding is an Excel import of the cardex or payroll. The sale is harder: the sector is relationship-driven and Spanish-only, and each state needs its own format. Leads are free from DOF sanction notices and state lists of authorised firms, and AMESP has 250 members.

results.one_line: About 1,450 real-estate firms and 845 car dealers must run a full SEPRELAD AML system that the free SIRO portal only receives filings for. SEPRELAD warned 1,692 of them in 2024 for missed filings, and no local tool does the whole job, so a Spanish-language compliance tool sold through registered auditors could reach about US$110k-135k a year by year 3, limited by low prices and warning-only enforcement.
results.gap: SIRO is a filing portal only. SEPRELAD's 2024 annual report shows: 1,238 real-estate firms and 454 car dealers warned for missing negative reports, operations reports (RO), the Annual Form (due 31 May), and the external audit and internal control reports. Only 526 real-estate firms and 357 car dealers sent the Annual Form, against about 1,451 and 845 fee payers. 532 of 2,042 SIRO registration requests were annulled for not meeting requirements. The new E-porandu help channel answered 855 questions in about 4.5 months, mostly on how to send a ROS or RO and on SIRO access. Small firms key in RO operation by operation, while larger ones can upload JSON. SEPRELAD ran 27 trainings for 533 participants. The portal keeps no KYC files, list checks, manual, risk matrix, internal evaluation or audit pack. A deadline tracker, KYC and deal register, document templates, JSON export and auditor export would fix this.
results.competitor_check: No Paraguayan product found. Pirani AML (Colombia) has a SEPRELAD guide page and a generic risk matrix, list screening (an add-on) and suspicious-operation reporting. It does not list Paraguay as a country, names no Paraguayan clients, does not cover the Annual Form, negative reports, RO JSON or Res 201/2020 templates, and does not publish prices, so it is a partial fit. Compliance Paraguay sells only a PEP database, price not published. theKYB offers screening data only, quote-only pricing. Law firms such as Ferrere and the registered auditors sell advice and audits; their fees are unverified. The incumbent is the free portal plus templates and consultants, which is an opening, not a killer.
results.price: About US$30 a month (about Gs 220k), or about US$360 a year, per firm. About US$20 a month per extra entity in a group. About US$100-150 a month (about US$1,500 a year) for an auditor or consultant plan with up to 30 client firms. An optional PEP and sanctions data add-on at about US$5-10 a month. Anchors: SEPRELAD's annual fee is about US$45, and a bookkeeping assistant costs Gs 3-6m a month. Auditor fees are unverified.
results.revenue: Real estate: 1,451 x 15% x US$360 = about US$78k. Car dealers: 845 x 10% x US$300 = about US$25k. Auditor and consultant licences: 20 x US$1,500 = US$30k, which partly overlaps with the firm counts (SEPRELAD admitted 64 new auditors in 2024; the full register size is unverified). Total about US$110k-135k a year in year 3. Non-profits (1,919 fee payers) are possible upside at a lower price.
results.ease: Medium. The build is easy to medium: a calendar, a KYC and deal register with thresholds, UN-list screening, Spanish templates and a JSON export for the RO. There is no SIRO API, and each sector needs its own templates. Onboarding is easy because small agencies have few deals. The sale is medium because buyers are price-sensitive and owner-run, but the warning letters are a clear trigger, the public lookup of registered subjects and auditors gives a lead list, and the registered auditors are an efficient channel.

results.one_line: Two 2 Aug 2026 Capital Market Authority circulars leave real work beyond the portal. One needs a protected 4-tab Excel file that the portal validates, plus a 50-year expert opinion for qualifying-donation gemachim. The other needs AML policy, risk assessment, board and training records. Israeli gemach software covers operations only, so a compliance layer fits, but about 170 small, price-sensitive buyers cap year-3 revenue near NIS 0.2-0.5m.
results.gap: Data circular 2026-10-5 starts 1 Jan 2027. It asks for balance sheet, P&L, cash flow by category, deposits, donations, credit and arrears by age, in a protected Excel file named Gmach_<licence>_QYY.xlsx. The portal (reportsportal.cma.gov.il) checks that the balance sheet balances and that minimum equity is met. It rejects files with hidden rows or wrong names. A filing counts only after an "accepted" e-mail. Deadlines: all licensees yearly by 30 June; extended licensees also half-yearly by 30 Sept; AML yearly report by 31 March. From 2028, gemachim taking qualifying donations must file a yearly external expert opinion with a 50-year forecast. The AML circular adds a policy and risk assessment reviewed yearly, board minutes kept 5 years, an AML officer, KYC/PEP and terror-list screening, and training logs for staff and volunteers. The portal only receives files. Mapping the books to the template, checking files before upload, a deadline calendar, AML registers and the modelling work are all left to the gemach. I found no direct user complaints about the portal. Pain shows indirectly: only 7 licences by Sept 2026, about 20 of 170+ applications "mature" in Dec 2025, and hearing letters now going out.
results.competitor_check: Three products serve gemach operations. Amud HaChesed (Malach Software) claims 12 years of service and wide use, but lists no features or prices. Moses Group covers the loan workflow, guarantors, deposits, donations and Masav direct debit; price on request. Gmach Beclick is an early-stage web app with placeholder stats and a dead pricing page. None mentions AML, Capital Market Authority reporting or template export. Generic lending software (CAV, Capterra listings) is built for interest-bearing lenders. I found no published gemach compliance package from advisers. Prices are hidden everywhere, so I could not judge them (unverified). These are partial incumbents, which makes this an opening. The risk is that Amud HaChesed adds an export to the template.
results.price:
My estimates (unverified):
- Basic licensee: NIS 250-500 a month (NIS 3,000-6,000 a year).
- Extended licensee: NIS 1,000-2,500 a month (NIS 12,000-30,000 a year).
- AML-officer or policy service add-on: NIS 1,000-3,000 a month.
- Expert-opinion model support: NIS 10,000-30,000 a year per qualifying-donation gemach.
- CPA offices: NIS 400 a month plus NIS 150 per client entity.
results.revenue:
Assume about 100 licensed by 2029 (85 basic, 15 extended), out of about 170 applicants (unverified).
- Software: 85 x 25% x NIS 4,500 = NIS 95,600, plus 15 x 33% (5 customers) x NIS 20,000 = NIS 100,000. Total about NIS 196,000 (about USD 53k).
- Services: 12 x NIS 18,000 = NIS 216,000, plus 3 x NIS 20,000 = NIS 60,000. With software, total about NIS 470,000 (about USD 127k).
- Upside if all 170 are licensed: about NIS 0.6m. That is 145 x 25% x 4,500 = 163k, plus 25 x 33% x 20,000 = 165k, plus services of about 276k.
results.ease: Build is medium. The template, field rules and validation checks are public, so a trial-balance or Excel import that outputs a validated file, plus AML registers, takes a few weeks. Pulling data from the operational systems needs an export or a partner. Selling is hard: it is a closed charedi community that needs Hebrew, trust, community endorsement and in-person sales. Buyers are few but can be named from the Authority's public register. The best channels are a reseller deal with Amud HaChesed or charedi CPA offices.

results.one_line: There is a real but small opening: a cheap tool that turns multi-channel booking exports into the monthly, per-premises figures that visitorlevy.scot asks for, and keeps the 5-year evidence file. It is easy to build and no incumbent does the whole job, but the Scottish market only supports about £20k-£100k a year unless England's percentage levy arrives.
results.gap: visitorlevy.scot is a manual entry form for registration, quarterly returns and payment. Each quarter it asks, for every month and every premises, for accommodation-only revenue, revenue booked before 1 Oct 2025 and revenue beyond night 5. The council can also ask for five monthly counts. It has no booking-data import (CSV/API unconfirmed). Its calculator is "not endorsed" and used at the user's own risk. It keeps no evidence records, even though the Act requires 5 years of records (s.28), with penalties for missing records (s.54) and inaccurate information (s.59), plus inspection (s.38) and council assessment (s.45). There is no agent or accountant login (unverified), and multi-council hosts must deal with each council separately. Pain is evidenced: about 8 minutes of manual correction per bill, STA and FSB complaints, and a Minister accepting that early non-compliance may come from providers learning the system. No late-filing data exists yet, because the first returns close on 30 Oct 2026.
results.competitor_check: The incumbents are partial and each works only inside its own booking system. Bookster (about £25-£44/month for up to 3 rentals, per Capterra, unverified) adds a levy uplift, but its return report was still "to be reviewed". freeonlinebooking has two levy reports, PMS price not stated, fit to portal fields unverified. Hop has a hotel-PMS finance report. freetobook and Roommaster show the levy to guests and publish guidance only. No levy feature was found at Eviivo, Little Hotelier, Lodgify or Guesty (unverified). Airbnb and Booking.com do not remit. No priced accountant service and no standalone multi-channel return-prep tool were found. Letting managers (Houst about 14% of nightly income) are buyers for a multi-owner tool, not competitors.
results.price: Single host: £6-£8 per property per month, or £25 per return (about £70-£100 a year). Anchors: a first late-return penalty of about £108-£398, 1-3 hours of work per quarter, an accountant at a likely £50-£150 per return (unverified), and £25-£44/month already spent on a PMS. The 2% retention is only about £30 a year on a £30k unit. Letting managers and accountants: £2-£3 per property per month, with a £30 monthly minimum.
results.revenue: Buyers: Edinburgh's 3,209 STL licences plus about 200 B&Bs and guest houses, and Glasgow, Aberdeen, Stirling and West Dunbartonshire from 2027. That gives an estimated 5,000-7,000 small liable persons and 30-60 letting managers by 2029. Base case: 6,000 x 5% = 300 x £80 = £24k, plus 25 managers x 60 properties x £30 = £45k, about £69k. Low case: 5,000 x 3% x £70 = £10.5k, plus 10 x 40 x £24 = £9.6k, about £20k. High case: about £100k in Scotland, plus English mayoral areas from about 2028-29 (unverified timing).
results.ease: Build is easy: OTA CSV parsers, a rules engine (rate, 5-night cap, pre-Oct-2025 exemption, check-out quarter, extras) and output for one national standard form. An MVP takes about 4-6 weeks. Onboarding is easy, because the host just uploads files with no integration. Selling is medium: demand peaks around each quarter's filing window, buyers have low value each, councils will not endorse tools, and the channels are ASSC, guest-house associations, ICAS accountants and letting managers.
results.killer: none (main threats: councils switching to flat per-night rates under s.6A, the portal adding CSV import, PMS vendors shipping matching reports, and OTA collection agreements)

results.one_line: Under the new CBK rules (LN 191 of 2026), about 281 licensed lenders and about 548 stalled applicants face document-heavy duties that the portal does not help with, and no local product covers them, so an NDTCP application kit plus a compliance tool at about KES 15k a month could reach roughly USD 115k–215k a year by year 3, as a small niche business.
results.gap: CBK's licensing portal and the BSA returns system only accept submissions. Applications stall on documents: 429 of 480 were "pending documentation" in 2024, about 548 were still under review in July 2026, and the lenders' association said members "lack clarity on what to submit". Ongoing duties need records the portal does not keep: CBK approval logs for rate changes with 30-day customer notices (regs 26 and 55), a complaints register on a 7-day/48-hour/30-day clock, annual agent approvals, CRB listing notices, and the 31 December fee and annual return, where a late fee doubles the annual charge to KES 1m or 500k and can lead to revocation. Lenders also face overlapping CBK, ODPC and CAK duties (DFSAK complaint), rising complaint numbers (CAK 67 to 355 a year), and BSA returns built from spreadsheet templates. Law firms and accountants need a multi-client view.
results.competitor_check: No local product does the whole job. The CBK portal and BSA only take submissions. Law firms (Bowmans, CDH, Oraro, CM Advocates) advise but publish no prices, so they are a channel more than a rival. SuperLMS (40 MFIs and digital lenders) claims "reports your regulator expects" but names no CBK return, complaints register, policy set or calendar, and shows no price. Lendsqr costs USD 0, 200 or 500 a month, with no listed regulatory features and no Kenya pricing shown. Trigarc Compliance (FNJ & Associates, Nairobi) is a generic compliance calendar with an audit trail, sold on quote, with no NDTCP content, policy library or complaints register. YouVerify and Zigram cover AML only. These are partial or generic offerings, which leaves an opening.
results.price: Application kit: KES 75k–150k one-off (about USD 580–1,160), with an optional partner-advocate review. Ongoing tool: KES 10k–20k a month per lender, planned at KES 180k a year. Adviser plan for up to 20 lender clients: KES 40k–60k a month, about KES 600k a year. Anchors: CBK fees are KES 100k to apply and KES 250k or 500k a year, with a doubled late fee. Lendsqr costs USD 200–500 a month. Licensed lenders hold a KES 165bn loan book. These prices are my estimates; I found no published consultant prices.
results.revenue: Year 3, at about KES 129 per USD. Recurring lenders: a pool of 600–800 (281 licensed plus 300–500 new, unverified) × 10–15% share = 60–120 lenders × KES 180k = KES 10.8m–21.6m. Adviser plans: 5–8 firms × KES 600k = KES 3.0m–4.8m. New-entrant and upgrade kits: 10–15 × KES 100k = KES 1.0m–1.5m. Total: KES 14.8m–27.9m, about USD 115k–215k a year. Year 1 one-off bonus from the March 2027 rush: 35–56 kits × KES 100k = KES 3.5m–5.6m.
results.ease: Medium. The build is easy: a policy generator, registers and a calendar, with no CBK integration. The content is harder, because it needs an advocate to draft or review policies against LN 191. Buyers are easy to target through CBK's public lender list, the DFSAK and DLAK associations, and law firms as resellers. Regtech sales cycles in Nairobi are said to run 90–270 days (unverified), which is too slow for the March 2027 rush unless the kit is sold through law firms. English is enough.

results.one_line: With no state portal and no local software, a register, reconciliation and inspection-pack app for about 3,300 armed security firms, about 5,000 other business firearm holders and about 300 dealers faces no real rival. Year-3 revenue could reach about R3.6m (about US$200k), but the sale is slow and inspectors may still insist on paper books.
results.gap: There is no SAPS portal for business holders or dealers (the court-ordered dealer link was never built). Firms keep bound ink books. Software would add daily issue/return reconciliation, licence, competency and Reg 21 training expiry alerts, multi-site views and a one-click inspection pack. The pain is real: PSIRA ran 2,411 firearm inspections in 2025/26 and suspended or withdrew 2,427 firms; the Durban raid found missing firearms and pencil entries; security firms lost 847 firearms in half a year. Reg 22 allows entries "written or printed in permanent ink", so printed numbered pages may qualify (unverified).
results.competitor_check: None found locally. CybateSoft appears to be a general software house, likely not South African, with no firearm product. Foreign armoury systems (NextGen IoT, FN SAM, ArmorerLink) are military or police tools, priced on quote, and do not print Reg 22 formats. Guarding SaaS sold in South Africa (Kolonell's guide: €4-9 per officer per month) has no armoury module. The real incumbents are paper books, Excel and in-house armourers. That is an opening.
results.price: Estimates: R500/month for a small armed security firm, R1,500/month for a mid-size multi-site firm, R1,000/month for a dealer, R400/month for a farm, outfitter or range. Blended about R800/month (R9,600/yr) for security firms. A possible consultant tier is about R2,500/month for up to 10 client firms (unverified). Optional inspection-readiness audits at R3,000-8,000.
results.revenue: Armed security firms 3,340 x 8% = 267 x R9,600 = R2.56m. Other business holders about 5,000 x 3% = 150 x R4,800 = R0.72m. Dealers about 300 x 10% = 30 x R12,000 = R0.36m. Total about R3.64m (about US$200k) from 447 customers, plus perhaps 10-20% from audits and setup. The buyer counts are old (2017) and unverified for today.
results.ease: Medium. The build is easy to medium: a register app with signatures, numbered PDF printouts, an append-only log and an offline mode, with no state API needed. Onboarding is medium: import the firearm list, put a tablet in each armoury, train the armourers. The sale is medium to hard: many fragmented, cash-strapped firms that worry about firearm data in the cloud and need assurance that inspectors will accept the output. Channels exist through SASA, training providers and PSIRA agents.

results.one_line: The real gap is the cellar evidence books, which the portal does not keep, but Czech tools already keep them for 2,490 to 3,800 Kč a year (VineOS, Vitipad), so a newcomer would be selling to about 1,300 small, price-sensitive wineries with a year-3 ceiling of roughly 1.3 to 1.9 million Kč (50,000 to 76,000 EUR).
results.gap: Portál farmáře / Registr vinic only takes the harvest, production and stock declarations. The winery has to keep the decree 88/2017 evidence books itself: intake, purchase slips, batch traceability and per-vessel cards. Court cases show fines for books that were late or incomplete and for batches that could not be traced. I found no current complaints about the portal. Low software adoption suggests many producers still use paper (unverified). Two openings remain: a done-for-you service for producers on paper, and multi-client use for enology or contract-winemaking firms. No incumbent mentions multi-client use.
results.competitor_check: Local products do the job and are cheap. Vitipad covers the books under the decree 88/2017 electronic-book rules for a flat 3,800 Kč a year, but it reports only "over 60 wineries" since 2015. VineOS produces the PDF wine book and pre-fills the ÚKZÚZ stock, production and Wine Fund reports. It has a free tier and costs 2,490 Kč a year for Pro, but it is a one-person project. Agrowin Sklepmistr does the job too, but its price is not published, and the subsidised Valtice course teaches it. Vinservis eVin costs 14,400 Kč a year hosted, which is expensive for small wineries. These are well-priced local products that do the whole job, which is a killer under the owner's criteria. They are small vendors, though, not polished leaders.
results.price: Software: 2,500 to 4,000 Kč a year for small wineries (set by Vitipad and VineOS). Up to about 12,000 to 14,400 Kč a year for medium wineries (set by eVin). A done-for-you service might fetch 4,000 to 8,000 Kč a year (unverified). Multi-client use might fetch 1,500 to 2,500 Kč per client a year (unverified). For comparison, the average small winery pays only 2,736 Kč a year in Wine Fund levy.
results.revenue: Small wineries: 1,061 x 10% x 3,500 Kč = 371,000 Kč. Medium wineries: 237 x 10% x 12,000 Kč = 284,000 Kč. Service: 100 clients x 6,000 Kč = 600,000 Kč (client count unverified). Total about 1.26 million Kč (about 50,000 EUR) a year. With 15% shares and 150 service clients, the ceiling is about 1.9 million Kč (about 76,000 EUR).
results.ease: Build: medium. The forms are fixed and one developer could build it, but it needs irreversible, author-stamped entries and must match VineOS on offline use, e-labels and ÚKZÚZ exports. Sale: hard. Buyers are small, rural and price-sensitive, and the incumbents get state-subsidised training at Valtice. The Wine Fund newsletter reaches more than 1,600 subjects, which helps. A service is easy to start but hard to scale because of the January filing peak.
results.killer: Cheap local products already do the whole job: Vitipad at 3,800 Kč a year and VineOS Pro at 2,490 Kč a year, with a free tier. Vitipad's roughly 60 customers in 10 years point to weak willingness to pay in a buyer base of about 1,300 levy payers.

results.one_line: There is real room for a cheap UIF add-on for brokers, covering the client file, risk rating, lease-threshold tracking, the monthly-report export and the self-assessment, because the portal only takes finished reports and no local product serves brokers; but weak enforcement and a deregulation draft limit the price and uptake, so the business is worth about USD 100-150k a year.
results.gap: The UIF's SRO+/SROMasivo only takes the finished monthly and annual reports as a bulk template. It does not keep the client file (10 years, refreshed every 1, 3 or 5 years by risk), rate client risk, screen PEPs, track the 300-SMVM lease total across operations, log alerts or the 15/150-day suspicious-report clock, keep the manual and training records, or build the two-yearly self-assessment. Current practice is static Word templates from colegios and Reporte Inmobiliario, plus Excel. There is portal pain in the same UIF system: FACPCE told the UIF on 31 Mar 2026 that the accountants' form was not available in time. Accountants acting as REI for several brokers have no shared evidence view.
results.competitor_check: There is no well-priced local product that does the job for brokers. CONLAFT S.R.L. was founded in May 2024, has 8 staff and 5 systems deployed, and targets mutuales, cooperatives and accountants. It claims a matrix, KYC, client file, monitoring and reports, but has no broker focus and publishes no prices. Real estate CRMs (Tokko USD 80-300 a month, Xintel, InmoPC) have no UIF module. Screening APIs (Didit) are only a component. Law firms (ST Abogados) do one-off work at unpublished prices. The FACPCE and DNRPI templates are free but written for accountants and registries. The notaries' colegio has its own self-assessment app; no broker colegio offers one. This is an opening, not a killer.
results.price: About USD 25-35 a month (USD 300-420 a year) per agency or sole broker, roughly 10-15% of a CRM bill. That compares with an annual licence fee of about ARS 650,000 and fines of ARS 0.8-135 million. A self-assessment pack would be about USD 150-300 per two-year cycle. An accountant or consultant seat would be about USD 60-100 a month for 10-15 broker clients. A colegio white-label deal would be about USD 10-25k a year, or USD 1-3 per member a month. All of these prices are unverified estimates.
results.revenue: Base case: 5,000 agencies that sell regularly x 5% x USD 360 = USD 90k, plus 40 accountant seats x USD 900 = USD 36k, plus 1 colegio deal at USD 15k. That gives about USD 140k a year. Low case: 5,000 x 2% x USD 300 = USD 30k, plus 15 x USD 900 = USD 13.5k, giving about USD 45k. High case with a CRM partnership and two colegio deals: USD 250k or more. Buyer counts are unverified; there are 35-40k licensed brokers and an estimated 10-25k obliged.
results.ease: Medium. Building it is medium-easy: forms, risk rules, reminders and an export in the UIF bulk-template format, with PEP screening from an API. Onboarding is easy because each agency sets up once. Selling is medium-hard because small brokers buy only when pushed, so the product needs channels: colegios (which already hand out model manuals), CRM vendors (which already hold the sale data) and REI accountants. Prices have to be indexed or quoted in USD.

results.one_line: About 400 Peruvian gaming firms must keep an AML operations register in software, track due-diligence and training cycles, and assemble a statistics-heavy annual report. No local tool covers the gaming-specific workflow (screening tools only), so a cheap tool sold to operators and their outsourced compliance officers could reach about US$185k a year, limited by the small buyer base and light enforcement.
results.gap: Portal PLAFT, ROSEL and SISDEL only receive filings. For online operators, Res. SBS 03622-2025 says the RO must be logged daily, in date order, in IT systems with a backup, then uploaded on an SBS template that only the registered officer can download (arts. 22.4, 22.6). The land-based equivalent is likely but unverified. Since 01015-2026 the land-based RO also covers all promo prize winners at any amount, plus cash-outs of US$2,500 or more. The IAOC (due 15 Feb, with the IAI as an annex) requires monthly RO, unusual-operation and ROS statistics, training counts, shareholder IDs and room locations. Other cycles to track: a 30-day induction with proof, yearly worker checks, 2-year supplier refresh and 3-year risk assessment. Corporate officers must file one IAOC per entity. PRCP publishes yearly guides on filing the IAOC, and 10 firms were fined in one year for missing it. I found no direct user complaints about the portals (unverified).
results.competitor_check: The incumbents are partial. Pirani AML (Colombian) covers due diligence and screening, but its Peru page says nothing on RO, IAOC or training, lists no gaming sector, and prices by quote. Inspektor, sold by PLAFT Suite and Risk Global Consulting, does list screening plus consulting packages aimed at mining, construction and real estate, with no prices published. Experian Listas PLAFT is screening only. verifica.id is a PEP/watch-list API on monthly plans with no public price and one ID per query; it also sells a MINCETUR gambling-ban (ludopatía) check. GBG and KYCAID do KYC for online operators. Law firms (PRCP, Caro, Grupo Contable) publish no prices. None covers the casino RO, promo winners, the induction tracker or the IAOC. Casino-management systems at large chains may capture cash-outs (unverified).
results.price: Estimates, unverified: single-room operator S/300 a month (S/3,600 a year); small chain S/800 a month; online operator S/1,200 a month; outsourced officer or consultant S/150 per client entity a month (minimum S/750); setup fee S/500. For comparison, the maximum fine is 8 UIT (S/44,000) and micro-firm outsourced bookkeeping costs about S/1,050 a month. Compliance-officer fees were not found.
results.revenue: Small land-based firms: 250 of about 325 x 30% = 75 x S/3,600 = S/270,000. Small chains: 50 x 25% = 12 x S/9,600 = S/115,200. Online: 91 x 15% = 14 x S/14,400 = S/201,600. Setup fees: 101 x S/500 = S/50,500. Total about S/637,000, or about US$185,000 a year at S/3.45 per US$. Upside not counted: other UIF-supervised sectors (real estate, vehicle dealers, notaries).
results.ease: Medium. The build is medium-easy: forms, registers, reminders and report templates, plus Excel/CMS import. The SBS RO template is gated behind Portal PLAFT, so a partner compliance officer is needed. Onboarding is easy for small rooms, and in tiny firms the general manager can act as officer (art. 5.4, online rule). The sale is medium: a small, known buyer list (MINCETUR register, Peru Gaming Show, SONAJA), the outsourced officers as a multiplier channel, and a yearly peak before the 15 Feb IAOC deadline. Trust and data security matter in an AML-exposed sector.

results.one_line: SEPRELAD warned 454 vehicle firms in 2024 and fined one in 2025, and only 32% are up to date on annual reports. Its SIRO portal only receives filings, and no local product prepares operation reports, keeps KYC and manual records or tracks deadlines. But the active base is only about 450 firms, so the case relies on auditor resale and reuse for real estate.
results.gap: SIRO receives registration, ROS, negative reports, operation reports (RO) and the annual form, but each firm has to prepare that data itself. In 2025, 453 vehicle firms reported 156,019 operations, about 344 each, under Res 196 Art. 31; whether SIRO takes bulk upload is unverified. SIRO keeps no KYC/PEP client files, manual, code of ethics, training records or deadline calendar. Its planned vehicle-sector risk-matrix module only asks firms to declare their manual, self-assessment and training. Evidence of pain: 454 vehicle firms warned in 2024 for missed objective duties (RN, RO, annual form, audit and internal-control reports); annual-report regularisation only 32% in 2025; 35 on-site inspections in 2025; 450-532 registration requests cancelled each year for not meeting SIRO requirements; SIRO training still running in October 2026. SIRO also carries an annual user fee (Res 30/2024), so it is not free. Auditors (64 admitted in 2024, 71 more recommended in 2025) need a multi-client view.
results.competitor_check: No local product does the whole job. SIRO is a filing channel only, though SEPRELAD is building a risk-matrix module for the vehicle sector that will absorb part of a risk-assessment feature. Compliance Paraguay sells only a 9,000+ PEP database; its price is not published. TheKYB and Shufti Pro are developer APIs for PEP and sanctions screening, not a Res 196 workflow. Law firms (Ferrere, Amaral) and registered auditors sell custom advice, manuals and audits at unpublished prices. The Argentine CONLAFT platform was seen only in a search snippet and has no sign of a Paraguay presence (unverified).
results.price: Single lot or dealer: USD 25-40 a month (USD 300-480 a year) plus a USD 100-150 setup fee. Larger CADAM importers: USD 80-150 a month. Auditors and accountants: USD 10-15 per client entity a month, or about USD 150 a month for 15 clients. All are estimates; no local benchmark prices for audits, manuals or outsourced compliance were found (unverified).
results.revenue: Vehicle sector: 450 active firms x 20% x USD 400 = USD 36k, plus about 1,000 other registered firms x 5% x USD 300 = USD 15k, for about USD 51k a year. Real estate on the same engine: 800 annual-form filers x 15% x USD 400 = USD 48k. Combined: about USD 100k a year by year 3. Shares are assumptions.
results.ease: Medium. Version 1 is a Spanish web app: sales and KYC log, RO export and validation, deadline calendar, manual templates and an evidence folder. The SIRO formats and the official Res 196 text are still unseen. Leads are easy to find through SEPRELAD's public register, CIVU and CADAM, and the best channel is the registered auditors. Buyers are price-sensitive, small and partly informal; the recent warnings and first fine give a timely pitch.

results.one_line: The free portals only take filings, and no local product keeps the 84-item non-profit compliance record set (funds register, SEPRELAD AML programme, donor ID files, forms A-E prep, the transparency page every six months), so there is a real gap. But the buyers are about 1,000 funded NGOs, church-linked bodies and their accountants, and the law is under court challenge, which gives about USD 50-115k in year 3.
results.gap: SIARA and the beneficial-owner register only take filings. They do not keep the records the law requires. Ley 7363 art. 8 requires a register of all funds and the actions they paid for, minutes and receipts kept ready for MEF. The SEPRELAD OSFL programme requires a compliance officer, a training plan, an annual work plan, income and spending registers, list screening, donor identification with ID copies at USD 1,000 or more and a source-of-funds statement at USD 10,000, PEP checks, mass-fundraising reports, and, at level 3, a manual, an ethics code, a risk assessment and an external audit. Other gaps: validating forms A-E before the 30 June sworn filing, the open-data fund-use page with history (31 July and 31 January), and a calendar spread over more than 13 registries (ICNL checklist lists 84 items). Evidence of pain: the bishops (April 2026) say compliance needs paid professionals at considerable cost and asked for a 12-month extension and free digital tools. In 2020 the Colegio de Contadores sought relief from an about Gs. 8M late fine, with thousands of bodies late. MEF funds NGOs in the budget only if their earlier accounts were closed satisfactorily. No evidence was found of SIARA technical errors.
results.competitor_check: None found that does the job. Spanish searches found no Paraguayan software for the OSFL funds register, the SEPRELAD programme, forms A-E or the transparency page. Foreign NGO tools (Capterra list, the Spanish 'Gestión de asociaciones') handle dues and cash only, with no localisation. Local accounting software (Contasys) targets tax law. Price benchmark: FacturaSend (SIFEN e-invoicing, also required of in-scope OSFL) costs Gs. 100,000 a month, about USD 13. Current practice is accountants and law firms, with no published fees. Possible threat: MEF adding free tools, which the bishops requested.
results.price: Funded NGO full pack: Gs. 200,000-300,000 a month (about USD 26-39). Small association (calendar, beneficial-owner file, transparency page): Gs. 80,000-100,000 a month. Accountant plan: Gs. 60,000-80,000 per client a month, with a minimum of 5 clients. One avoided fine of about Gs. 8M covers about 3 years of the full pack.
results.revenue: Funded NGOs: 1,000 (unverified; 114 are on the 2025 state budget) x 15% = 150 x Gs. 250k x 12 = Gs. 450M (about USD 59k). Accountant channel: 40 firms x 10 clients = 400 x Gs. 70k x 12 = Gs. 336M (about USD 44k). Church-linked bodies: 300 x 20% = 60 x Gs. 150k x 12 = Gs. 108M (about USD 14k). Total about Gs. 894M, or about USD 117k. The low case (half the shares and accountants) is about USD 50-60k.
results.ease: Build is easy to medium: registers, checklists, templates, a calendar, a static open-data page and a multi-client dashboard, with no SIARA API, so filing stays copy and paste. The AML manual and risk templates need a local compliance expert. Onboarding is easy. The sale is medium to hard: the buyers are spread out, short of money and hostile to the law. The best channel is accountants (Colegio de Contadores), with the budget-transfer list as leads.

results.one_line: About 6,500 private kindergartens must be licensed from 2027 (with existing ones phased in to 2030), and no local product or priced consultant offers a readiness check, so a low-priced readiness pack that becomes a subscription for records and inspection readiness has an open gap, though it can only earn roughly US$60-255k a year.
results.gap: The eGov and elicense.kz portal only takes the application. A commission then checks the documents and visits the site. Nothing checks readiness before filing. The rules are spread across licensing, land, construction, sanitary and fire agencies, and regions apply them differently (informburo, 1 Oct 2026). The inspection scope is wide: sanitary, fire, CCTV, security, food and programmes (24.kz, 1 Sep 2026). Unannounced inspections have been allowed since Feb 2026. Teachers must keep recurring plans, the cyclogram and individual development plans. Staff categories and training hours need tracking. The state Indigo/ED24 apps handle attendance and funding only, and users complain about them.
results.competitor_check: None found that does the job. Ybcase is a general licensing consultant with no preschool package and no published price. Dogovor24 sells only generic templates. BALAM, a parent app, and Sadik (Global-Soft, likely Russian, free, under 1,000 downloads) have no licensing features. ED24/Indigo are state-paid attendance and funding systems with no readiness features. Their developer is the most likely to bundle a readiness module later (unverified).
results.price: Readiness check plus document pack: 50,000-100,000 tenge one-off (about US$100-200). Subscription: 8,000-15,000 tenge a month per site (about US$16-30), under 0.5% of the revenue of a 100-child kindergarten that takes in 3-7 million tenge a month (average fee about 30,000 tenge a month, private ones 70,000 or more). Consultants and chains: 25,000-50,000 tenge a month for up to 10 sites (unverified). All are estimates, since no market price was found.
results.revenue: Base case: 6,500 private kindergartens x 6% = 390 x 120,000 tenge a year = 46.8M, plus 300 one-off packs x 60,000 = 18M. Total about 65M tenge, roughly US$130k. Good case: 650 x 150,000 = 97.5M plus 400 x 75,000 = 30M, total about 128M tenge, roughly US$255k. Low case: 3% at 96,000 = 18.7M plus about 10M, total about 29M tenge, roughly US$58k.
results.ease: Medium. The software is simple: a questionnaire, a red/amber/green report, templates, a staff register with alerts and plan templates, with no state integration. The effort is in content: Russian and Kazakh versions, tracking Order 473/268 and notes for each region. Onboarding is easy. Selling to small, low-tech owners across 17 regions is the hard part. The channels are Atameken, the private-kindergarten associations and Instagram/WhatsApp owner groups.

results.one_line: goAML only handles registration and filing, and no Slovak tool covers the ongoing work: multi-source beneficial-owner (KUV) evidence, PEP and sanctions checks with an audit trail, risk scoring, the §20 programme and records. A cheap Slovak-law AML desk could fill that gap, but a Czech tool (AML PROOF, EUR 3-5 per check) caps prices, enforcement is light and buyers are a few thousand tiny firms, so it suits a side product earning about EUR 90k a year.
results.gap: goAML is a filing channel only: registration, unusual-transaction (NOO) reports and XML upload. Login uses two-factor authentication through Google Authenticator, and the manual has an account-reset chapter. Setting up access takes a few days. Since 1 Jun 2026, firms must check every client's beneficial owner against several reliable sources, and the portal does nothing for this. The FSJ says a client's own statement on PEP or sanctions status is not enough, and it points to EU, UN and OFAC lists and paid databases that small firms cannot afford. Manual checks leave no time stamp or source, which is near worthless at inspection. In the FSJ survey, 39% of agencies kept no record of internal NOO reviews and 23% did not vet staff. Programmes need rewrites for Act 73/2026 and again for the EU AMLR in July 2027. Accounting firms with many corporate clients have no per-client file or re-check reminders. No user complaints about goAML itself were found.
results.competitor_check:
No Slovak product does the whole job (as far as public sources show).
- goAML: free, but filing only.
- AKMV and other law firms: one-off documents from EUR 600, or EUR 130 per hour. No software, no updates, no goAML help. Partial, and a possible partner.
- FinStat AML: a PEP database via portal or API under contract. Price not public (403). A data source, not a workflow.
- Sumsub: built for larger, fintech-type buyers.
- AML PROOF (Czech): a full workflow (client ID, screening, risk scoring, internal policy, reports, audit trail, training) with no monthly fee, EUR 3 per individual check and EUR 5 per company check, internal policy for CZK 990, training CZK 490 per person per year. It has a Slovak-language page with EUR prices, but it covers only Czech law (no Slovak act, FSJ, goAML or RPVS). It is the main threat and the price anchor.
- Codamore "JUDICIUM": a Slovak AML app for small accounting firms, seen only in a LinkedIn search snippet. Unverified.
- KROS: no AML module found (not confirmed absent).
results.price:
- Small agency or sole-trader accountant: EUR 9-15 per month (about EUR 100-180 per year), including the programme template, a yearly update and about 20 checks. Extra checks at EUR 2-4.
- Accounting firm with 30-150 corporate clients: EUR 30-60 per month (EUR 360-720 per year), priced by number of client files.
- Programme-only package: EUR 99-199 one-off, against EUR 600+ for a law-firm pack.

These prices are capped by AML PROOF's EUR 3-5 per check. Buyers today pay EUR 600+ to lawyers or EUR 130 per hour, and fines averaged about EUR 10k (one accountant was fined EUR 50k in 2025). All of these prices are unverified with buyers.
results.revenue:
Base case, year 3, about EUR 90k per year:
- Small firms: 5,500 x 5% = 275 customers x EUR 150 = EUR 41,250
- Multi-client accounting firms: 1,000 x 8% = 80 customers x EUR 500 = EUR 40,000
- Extra checks and programme packages: about EUR 10,000 (unverified)

The low case is about EUR 30k (2-3% share, lower prices). The high case is about EUR 180k (10% share, with a chamber or accounting-software partner).

Buyer counts are unverified:
- Agencies: 1,000-2,000; 223 answered the FSJ questionnaire.
- Bookkeeping firms with external clients: about 4,000 active. The NACE 69.20 aggregator lists 57k records, but that includes inactive and side-line firms.
- Tax advisers: about 1,000. Auditors: several hundred.
results.ease:
Medium.
- Build: medium. The core is a client file, the public EU sanctions list import, business-register and RPVS lookups, a PDF inspection pack and a programme template that needs Slovak lawyer review. The PEP data source costs extra (FinStat).
- Onboarding: easy. A web app with no integration needed.
- Sale: medium to hard. Buyers are tiny and the inspection risk is low (about 10 on-site checks in 2025, EUR 142k in total fines), so fear alone will not sell it. Bulk channels exist: NARKS and ZRKS (the FSJ itself distributed its survey through them), SKDP, SKCU, and accounting-software vendors.
results.killer: None today. The near-killer is AML PROOF, a cheap Czech tool that does the whole job under Czech law and already has a Slovak-language page with EUR prices. If it adds Slovak law, the opening largely closes. The unverified Codamore "JUDICIUM" Slovak app must also be checked.
